The City of Boroondara is seeking a suitably experienced provider to work with Council to develop a Service Review Framework (Part 1), with the option to subsequently extend the Framework to incorporate a Service Planning Approach (Part 2).

Part 1 – Service Review Framework

1. Part 1.A – Development of the Framework

The provider will develop a practical, fit-for-purpose Service Review Framework that establishes a consistent approach to planning and undertaking service reviews across Council, including the methodology, tools and supporting resources required to undertake future service reviews.

The Framework should complement Council’s Benefits Framework by supporting the identification, assessment and tracking of benefits from review recommendations, and enable insights and opportunities identified through reviews to inform ongoing service improvement.

The Framework, associated resources and intellectual property will be owned by Council and will provide the basis for establishing a panel of suitably qualified providers to undertake future service reviews on Council’s behalf.

2. Part 1.B – Pilot of the Framework

As part of Part 1, the successful provider will be required to pilot the Service Review Framework with one small Council service. The pilot will provide an opportunity to test the Framework, methodology and tools in practice and refine them based on the experience of undertaking a review.

The pilot should demonstrate how the Framework can be practically applied and help ensure the final Framework is fit-for-purpose, scalable and capable of being applied consistently across Council.

Part 2 – Service Planning Approach

As an optional next phase, Council may choose to engage the successful provider to extend the Service Review Framework to incorporate a Service Planning Approach.

Part 2 is not guaranteed and would only proceed at Council’s discretion. It is dependent on the development of Council’s Service Catalogue, which is currently underway, and would therefore be undertaken after Part 1 has been completed.

Reverse Brief

Council is seeking a reverse brief from respondents that demonstrates their understanding of the opportunity across both Part 1 and the potential Part 2, recommends an appropriate approach and sequencing, and identifies any refinements, considerations or dependencies that Council should take into account. This should include how the proposed Framework would complement Council’s Benefits Framework and support ongoing service improvement.

Respondents should outline their proposed approach to developing and piloting the Service Review Framework and, where relevant, their proposed approach to subsequently incorporating Service Planning. Respondents are encouraged to draw on their experience in service review and service planning to propose an approach that will deliver a practical, scalable and sustainable Framework for use across Council.

Overview
Future Generation is a joint venture created specifically to build Snowy 2.0 on behalf of Snowy Hydro Limited. We bring the combined engineering expertise of three companies – Italy’s Salini Impregilo, Australian-based Clough and US-based Lane Construction. Our team’s pair local expertise with global experience.



Snowy 2.0 will supercharge the Snowy Scheme’s existing hydro-electric generation and large-scale storage capabilities. The fast-start, on-demand generation of pumped-hydro and Snowy 2.0’s massive storage capacity will be vital as more intermittent, renewable energy sources such as wind and solar come online and coal-fired power stations retire.



Snowy 2.0 will add 2,000 megawatts of energy generation and provide 175 hours of storage for the National Electricity Market (NEM), enough to ensure the stability and reliability of the system during prolonged weather events, such as wind or solar ‘droughts’.

Snowy Hydro already plays a critical role in ensuring system stability and at times of peak demand, we keep the lights on. Snowy 2.0 will enhance our existing capability and ensure that we can continue to provide increased stability and security to the energy market well into the future.



The project links two existing Scheme dams, Tantangara and Talbingo, through tunnels and an underground power station with pumping capabilities. Hydro-power will be generated by falling water spinning Snowy 2.0’s giant reversible turbines, which can also pump water in the opposite direction.

Snowy 2.0’s pumping capabilities work in a ‘closed’ system – water is recycled between the upper dam (Tantangara) and lower dam (Talbingo) so the same water can be used to generate power more than once, making the most of available water. Snowy Hydro already has pumped-hydro capabilities at the Tumut 3 Power Station - it is proven technology used across the world



The ability to store water and generate power on-demand means Snowy 2.0 can be ‘switched on’ very quickly. Snowy 2.0 will pump water using the excess electricity in the system at times of low demand. Then, when energy is needed most, the stored water will be used to generate electricity within minutes.

For example, if the wind is blowing in the middle of the night when consumers are asleep, Snowy 2.0 can use the wind energy to pump and then store the water in the upper dam. When households wake up and the demand for energy soars, Snowy 2.0 can quickly generate energy for the grid.

The first power produced from Snowy 2.0 is expected in late 2024-25, with progressive commissioning on the six units. Snowy 2.0’s operating life is expected to be consistent with the Snowy Scheme’s existing assets, which continue to operate reliably many decades after installation.

NIGHT RISE is a new Fremantle Biennale initiative that will bring together contemporary art experiences, artists and cultural leaders with the dark sky places, stories and communities of Western Australia.

Over 80% of the world’s population now live in areas where they cannot see the stars. Across Australia astrotourism and initiatives focussed on protecting darkness are growing rapidly, as ever-greater numbers of people seek out starlight and naturally occurring phenomena such as eclipses, solstices and rare astral happenings.

Western Australia is one of the world’s most remarkable places to experience the night sky and its celestial movements. NIGHT RISE explores how arts and culture can contribute unique perspectives, experiences and ways of connecting to our vast dark sky environments.

NIGHT RISE is currently in a research and creative development period across four WA regions – the Wheatbelt, Gascoyne, Murchison and the Kimberley. In its delivery NIGHT RISE will present new place-responsive artworks, cultural experiences and community initiatives coalescing in a series of destination events.

The Fremantle Biennale is a Western Australian arts organisation commissioning and presenting ambitious site-responsive contemporary art. Through a biennial festival and year-round program, we facilitate and create opportunities, connections and transformative experiences between artists, audiences and place.

Expressions of Interest are now open for the first Night Rise project: Wheatbelt Observatories.

The Fremantle Biennale is calling for Expressions of interest from artists and architects to create a series of sky-led observatories across Western Australia’s Wheatbelt region.

Following extensive consultation with communities across the region we are seeking ambitious ideas from collaborations between artists and architects to imagine singular observatories and built forms for five sites across the Wheatbelt.

The proposed observatories will explore both nocturnal and diurnal experiences, creating places to gather, shelter, look, listen and connect with the sky and horizon. Combining permanent and temporary works, the observatories will form a constellation and landmark dark sky trail that will be activated by the Biennale and each community through public programs, seasonal gatherings, storytelling, performances and other cultural experiences.

Led by the Office for Early Childhood Development (OECD), the Strategy ensures that the universal rollout of 3-year-old preschool from 2026 empowers Aboriginal children and their families.

The Strategy is complex, comprising multiple cross-cutting long-term initiatives with distinct aims and objectives. This complexity requires a carefully considered and clearly articulated approach to measuring the Strategy’s impact over time, including what will be evaluated, how success will be measured, and when evaluation activities will occur.

To this end, the OECD is seeking a qualified and experienced South Australian Aboriginal business supplier to develop an Evaluation Framework that provides comprehensive guidance on how to assess the Strategy’s impact. The requirements of the Framework are twofold: it must be developed with evaluative rigour while being firmly grounded in and guided by the principles of Aboriginal leadership and self-determination.

The Framework will be developed over a 6-month engagement to establish a strategic, cross-program approach to evaluation. It will be grounded in Aboriginal ways of knowing, being and doing, alongside Western evaluation approaches applied in a complementary manner. It will be developed through a co-design approach with the Aboriginal Co-design Governance Group (ACGG), the OECD Aboriginal Leadership Committee and relevant stakeholders to embed Aboriginal governance and voice throughout the framework’s design.

Operating at a whole-of-strategy level, the Framework will establish core principles, parameters and outcomes to guide program-level evaluation. It will provide guidance on timing, methodologies, key themes and questions across initiatives as a cohesive package, rather than at an individual program level. In doing so, it will define what will be evaluated, how, and when.

To be considered for this engagement, it is a requirement that at least 51% of the work is contracted to, and undertaken by, an Aboriginal-owned organisation. Overview
Future Generation is a joint venture created specifically to build Snowy 2.0 on behalf of Snowy Hydro Limited. We bring the combined engineering expertise of three companies – Italy’s Salini Impregilo, Australian-based Clough and US-based Lane Construction. Our team’s pair local expertise with global experience.



Snowy 2.0 will supercharge the Snowy Scheme’s existing hydro-electric generation and large-scale storage capabilities. The fast-start, on-demand generation of pumped-hydro and Snowy 2.0’s massive storage capacity will be vital as more intermittent, renewable energy sources such as wind and solar come online and coal-fired power stations retire.



Snowy 2.0 will add 2,000 megawatts of energy generation and provide 175 hours of storage for the National Electricity Market (NEM), enough to ensure the stability and reliability of the system during prolonged weather events, such as wind or solar ‘droughts’.

Snowy Hydro already plays a critical role in ensuring system stability and at times of peak demand, we keep the lights on. Snowy 2.0 will enhance our existing capability and ensure that we can continue to provide increased stability and security to the energy market well into the future.



The project links two existing Scheme dams, Tantangara and Talbingo, through tunnels and an underground power station with pumping capabilities. Hydro-power will be generated by falling water spinning Snowy 2.0’s giant reversible turbines, which can also pump water in the opposite direction.

Snowy 2.0’s pumping capabilities work in a ‘closed’ system – water is recycled between the upper dam (Tantangara) and lower dam (Talbingo) so the same water can be used to generate power more than once, making the most of available water. Snowy Hydro already has pumped-hydro capabilities at the Tumut 3 Power Station - it is proven technology used across the world



The ability to store water and generate power on-demand means Snowy 2.0 can be ‘switched on’ very quickly. Snowy 2.0 will pump water using the excess electricity in the system at times of low demand. Then, when energy is needed most, the stored water will be used to generate electricity within minutes.

For example, if the wind is blowing in the middle of the night when consumers are asleep, Snowy 2.0 can use the wind energy to pump and then store the water in the upper dam. When households wake up and the demand for energy soars, Snowy 2.0 can quickly generate energy for the grid.

The first power produced from Snowy 2.0 is expected in late 2024-25, with progressive commissioning on the six units. Snowy 2.0’s operating life is expected to be consistent with the Snowy Scheme’s existing assets, which continue to operate reliably many decades after installation.

Building Snowy 2.0

The project will involve underground excavation and tunneling works between Tantangara and Talbingo dams to depths of up to one kilometre. There will be surface works in several locations including intake-outlet structures at Talbingo and Tantangara dams, surge shafts and tunnel portal sites. A number of supporting works are also required, such as establishing or upgrading access roads, and electricity connections to construction sites.



CONSTRUCTION

About 27km of power waterway tunnels will be constructed to link Tantangara and Talbingo dams. The tunnels are about 10m in diameter and entirely concrete-lined to ensure construction safety, operational longevity and low maintenance. Intake and outlet structures will be constructed at both dams.

The power station complex will be located approximately 800m underground. Two main caverns will be excavated:

? Machine hall - approx. 240m (long) x 50m (high) x 30m (wide).

? Transformer hall - approx. 200m (long) x 50m (high) x 20m (wide).

Six galleries run between the two halls and carry cables that connect the generators with the transformers.

To reinforce the structure, rock bolts of 15 to 20m in length will be drilled into the rock at the top and sides of each cavern. Up to three tunnel boring machines, as well as drill and blast techniques, will be used for tunneling and excavation.



MECHANICAL AND ELECTRICAL

The power station will house six reversible Francis pump-turbine and motor-generator units. Three units will be synchronous (fixed) speed and three will be asynchronous (variable) speed. The units will be arranged in the power station in alternating order. There will be a single inclined pressure tunnel that is concrete-lined and will divert water into six steel-lined penstocks (the tunnels that feed water into the generating units).
